components.text: Whether secular-humanist values, distinguished from bare atheism, can contribute to a better world.
The decisive demand is the distinction between bare atheism and the positive commitments of secular humanism.
The claimed causal inference from removing God to intensified exclusionary secular moralism.
The decisive demand is whether atheism or removal of God causally explains punitive secular dogmatism.
Whether a specified secular-humanist program can contribute constructively beyond bare atheism.
Whether exclusionary dogmatism is attributable to atheism rather than separate ideologies.
The decisive earlier demand is to evaluate secular humanism separately from atheism's lack of positive program.
The additional demand is whether adverse secular conduct is caused by atheism or by independent ideological dogmatism.
Whether reported flourishing establishes a distinctive benefit of intrinsic religiosity.
Whether removing God produces heightened exclusionary moralism.
The decisive demand is whether observed flourishing is specifically attributable to intrinsic religion rather than reporting effects or community support.
The earlier claim that secular public life redirects religious impulses into exclusion is not materially answered here.
Whether community rather than intrinsic religion explains the reported benefits.
Whether secular humanism supplies a positive program beyond atheism.
Whether dogmatism arises from ideology rather than atheism.
The decisive demand is whether community alone explains the association or whether intrinsic transcendent orientation adds something distinctive.
Whether community mechanisms explain benefits without establishing religious truth.
Whether secular humanism can supply a positive program beyond atheism.
Whether dogmatism stems from political ideology rather than atheism.
The contacted demand is that practical or communal benefits do not establish the truth of the religion producing them.
The distinction between bare atheism and secular humanism's positive commitments is not resolved by insisting on truth.
The rival attribution of dogmatism to political ideology rather than atheism is not addressed.
Whether orientation toward something higher and transcendent is distinctively religious.
Whether moral practice must be grounded in the truth of Christianity.
Whether intrinsic religiosity produces distinctive social benefits.
The decisive demand is whether awe, higher commitment, and community require a supernatural transcendent orientation.
The broad empirical claim about intrinsic religion's measured flourishing is not directly tested.
The demand that moral practice be grounded in a true account of reality is not answered.
Whether secular humanism can sustain awe, higher commitment, social concern, and community.
Whether secular humanism offers a positive program beyond bare atheism.
Whether community rather than religion explains social benefits.
The decisive earlier demand is whether secular people can sustain awe, higher commitments, concern, and community without supernatural belief.
The rival community and self-report explanations for religious benefits are not answered.
Whether Christianity uniquely originates and secures universal dignity for weak and excluded people.
Whether useful moral practice must rest on Christianity's truth.
Whether intrinsic religiosity yields distinctive flourishing.
The decisive demand is whether Christianity uniquely originates or secures the inherited ideal of protecting weak people and outsiders.
The additional demand is whether useful moral practice must remain grounded in Christianity's truth claims.
The empirical claim about intrinsic religiosity and flourishing is not addressed.
Whether Christianity supplies the true ground required for workable moral practice.
Whether Christianity secures universal concern for human beings.
Whether intrinsic religion produces distinctive flourishing.
The decisive demand is whether invoking Christian truth provides an accessible ground for moral concern and obligation.
The additional demand is whether divine concern uniquely secures human dignity and interests.
The empirical distinctiveness of transcendent orientation is not addressed.
Whether a divine premise adds a demonstrated foundation beyond human concern.
Whether secular humanism can inherit Christian moral ideas without their supernatural source.
Whether secular people can sustain awe and higher commitment.
The decisive demand is whether divine identification adds a defensible foundation beyond direct human concern and well-being.
The claim that secular humanists can inherit moral ideas without supernatural premises is challenged only indirectly.
The empirical community explanation of religious benefits is not addressed.
Whether only divine identification can securely ground human dignity and exceptional concern.
Whether Christianity uniquely protects universal dignity and the weak.
Whether moral practice requires Christianity's truth.
The decisive demand is whether human interests and dignity require divine identification rather than a human-centered foundation.
The claimed Christian source of universal concern is contacted through inheritance and comparative revision.
The demand for Christian truth is answered by arguing that useful ideas can be retained without the God premise.
Whether centering human interests and revising harmful traditions supplies a better foundation.
Whether shared human concern is a sufficient foundation without God.
Whether humans can preserve and revise inherited moral ideas.
The decisive demand is whether centering human interests reliably protects every human, especially those outside the powerful group's narrowed concern.
The earlier claim that shared human concern is a sufficient starting point is challenged by concern's tendency to narrow.
The capacity to inherit and revise ideas is not directly denied or assessed.
Whether human-centered concern can provide a workable foundation protecting people amid disagreement.
Whether the incarnation supplies a necessary foundation for dignity.
Whether an asserted true Christian ground is needed before moral deliberation.
The decisive demand is what practical foundation permits moral deliberation and protection when metaphysical agreement is unavailable.
The divine-identification ground is challenged as undemonstrated and inaccessible as shared premises.
The insistence on a true Christian ground is contacted through the demand that the God premise be demonstrated.
Whether immense human value requires intrinsic dignity conferred through divine identification.
Whether rights for all humans require value independent of human judgment.
Whether equal dignity must be intrinsic and Christian-grounded.
The decisive demand is whether immense human value requires intrinsic value conferred by God or the universe.
The practical concern about protecting weak people is acknowledged only indirectly through immense human valuation.
The equal-dignity claim is challenged at the level of intrinsic grounding but not its inclusive practical norm.
Whether human-centered morality can criticize systems that narrow the moral circle against weak people.
Whether only Christian dignity can condemn oppressive exclusion.
Whether intrinsic divine dignity is required for moral assessment.
The decisive demand is whether a fallible human-centered method can condemn exclusion and protect an appropriately broad moral circle.
The need for divine intrinsic dignity is answered by offering consequence-based moral assessment.
The concern for weak and excluded people is contacted through analysis of oppression, slavery, and Nazism.
Whether secular consequence reasoning can condemn oppressive systems without Christian formation.
Whether humane ideas can be inherited while Christianity is discarded.
Whether secular humanism comparatively improves on Christianity.
The decisive demand is whether fallible deliberation and wellbeing alone explain recognition and resistance of radically exclusionary evil.
The claim that secular humanism can inherit Christian ideas is indirectly supported rather than defeated by the historical-formation claim.
The comparative capacity to reject harmful Christian doctrines is not directly addressed.
Whether immense human valuation can exist without objective intrinsic value.
Whether shared concern alone supplies a workable moral foundation.
Whether consequences and corrigibility can ground moral criticism.
The decisive demand is whether shared agreement and natural human concern are sufficient to ground objective ethical obligation.
The denial of intrinsic value is contacted by asserting an objective moral realm irreducible to human preference.
The practical corrigibility of wellbeing judgments is not directly denied or explained.
Whether atheism's lack of a positive program is answered by adding secular-humanist values.
Whether secular humanism is comparatively better despite offering no guarantee.
Whether secular inquiry can protect weak people through revisable consequence reasoning.
The decisive demand is to distinguish atheism's lack of positive content from secular humanism's proposed moral commitments.
The claim that secular humanism is comparatively better is attacked through alleged social costs of abandoning Christianity.
The capacity of secular wellbeing reasoning to protect vulnerable people is challenged but not directly analyzed.
The distinction between immense relational value and intrinsic value is not expressly answered.
